title: Poor in spirit, even if rich (III.14–III.16)
hook: a spare coat in your closet, a thin one on someone you know: do you have your things, or do they have you?
tomorrow: Mia says Sofia only texts when she needs advice. is she right?

segments.voice: Yesterday, busy without anxiety: care, in order, one hand held while the other picks berries. The line was careful, not anxious.

A second coat in the back of your closet, barely worn. Someone you know is getting through the winter in a thin one. Nobody's asking you for anything. So what do you do with the spare when someone else's is falling apart? Francis de Sales would call it a small test of a big question. Philothea has a household, money, things to look after, and he never tells her to sell it all. He tells her where to keep it.
screen: `A SPARE COAT. A THIN ONE.` → `NOBODY'S ASKING.` → `WHERE DO YOU KEEP IT?`

segments.voice: First, the beatitude, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." Francis asks where that poverty lives, and answers: in the heart. Riches can sit in your house and your purse without sitting in your heart. A psalm says it plainly: "if riches abound, set not your heart upon them." Second, the test. Look after what you have, he says, carefully, even make it fruitful, since it's been entrusted to you. Then notice what happens when you lose some of it. If a loss leaves you deeply upset and anxious, the heart was holding on tighter than you knew. Third, the practice, for someone who isn't poor. Give some of it away, freely, and keep doing it. He goes further: serve the poor yourself, with your own hands, not only with your purse, and be glad to go without a little. Fourth, the other side of the page. For someone who really is poor, he says, poverty borne gently can be rich in spirit too. Either way, the question isn't how much is in the house. It's who's holding whom.
screen: `BLESSED ARE THE POOR IN SPIRIT.` · `IN THE HOUSE, NOT THE HEART.` · `THE TEST OF A LOSS.` · `GIVE, WITH YOUR OWN HANDS.` · then, large: `HAVING WITHOUT BEING HAD.`

segments.voice: Look at one thing you own and like: a jacket, a mug, a book. Hold it, or rest your eyes on it, through the sit, and ask honestly whether you have it or it has you. If something comes to mind that you could give away, let it come.
Poor in spirit. Riches, if you have them, kept in the house and out of the heart; and something always being given away.
Your line: having without being had. The coat is yours; you are not the coat's. Take care.
